newsitem.title: USA: Wall Street begins August on the defensive.
newsitem.headline: Wall Street begins August on the defensive.

text.p: Stocks finished July with a record gain for a month, but they entered the dog days of August on a defensive note.
"The mood has changed," said Hugh Johnson, chief investment officer at First Albany Corp. "I think every investor small or large will start the week on edge."
Stocks headed lower on Friday after unexpectedly strong July economic data revived lurking inflation fears.

The nation's jobless rate dropped back to a 25-year low of 4.8 percent last month, the government said Friday. The surprising upturn in the labour market, coupled with reports showing solid growth in consumers' incomes and a booming manufacturing sector, sent the bond market reeling and gave investors an excuse to take profits in stocks.
The Dow Jones industrial average ended Friday down 28.57 points at 8,194.04 after sinking to a low of 8,103.40. For the week, the blue-chip index rose 80.60 points.
Although the Dow regained much of its lost ground at the end of the day, the economic news left Wall Street jittery.

"Yes, we made a recovery in the last half hour but that doesn't mean professional investors are any less edgy," said Johnson. "There was more reason to fear being overvalued at the end of the day than at the beginning of the day. Don't let that recovery fool you."
"The news (Friday) was very troubling," Johnson said. "It appears as though, as we start the month, the economy is picking up some."
July was the Dow's best month so far this year as the index topped 8,000 for the first time.
For the month, the blue-chip indicator was up 549.82 points, or 7.2 percent, as the market navigated successfully through second-quarter earnings and the Federal Reserve kept interest rates steady.
It was also the heaviest trading month on record with nearly 12 billion shares changing hands.
Many on Wall Street felt that the market was overpriced and due for a bit of backpeddling, but next week will tell whether Friday's statistics provide the impetus for a more sustained downturn.
"If the bond market gives some further ground the market should go down a next week," said Harry Laubscher of Tucker Anthony.
But First Albany's Johnson noted that the market has had several setbacks, only to resume climbing with renewed vigour afterwards.

"We have had bouts of downturn every few months for some time," he said. "We may be in for a bout of declining stocks now. But every time the mutual funds and small investors have come roaring back in."
"Is this the death knell for the bull market?" said Phil Orlando of Value Line Asset Management. "I don't think so. I don't think the Fed's position (on interest rates) has changed one iota."

But Johnson disagreed. "A week ago few believed the Fed would raise rates in August or September," he said. "Today there are many strategists who are thinking it seriously. The chances are much better for an increase."

"The market is likely to see some some selling early next week," said Alan Ackerman, senior vice president at Fahnestock & Co. "The market is seeing some inflation fears. A setback such as today does not necessarily indicate the bull market is over but the range is likely to be tight next week."
